summary: This standards-track memo proposes a way to find a URI associated with a solicitation class keyword from the No Soliciting SMTP extension (RFC 3865). The keywords are reversed domain names, such as org.example.adv.

eli5.summary: Advertising emails can carry a label saying what kind they are. This document says how to look up what that label means.

questions: what is a solicitation class keyword
how to look up a no-solicit keyword
what is a naptr record used for
how does the no-solicit naptr service work
subtitle: How to turn a reversed-domain spam label into a web page that explains what the label means.

tldr.problem: RFC 3865 lets mail carry solicitation class keywords such as com.example.adv, but treats them as opaque labels, so a recipient has no standard way to learn what a keyword means.
tldr.mechanism: The keyword is converted into a domain name and looked up as a DNS NAPTR record, whose REGEXP field holds a URI of a page that explains the keyword.
tldr.outcome: The design deliberately maps a keyword to nothing more than a URI, with no required format for the explanation, and it warns that DNS compromise, misleading keywords and lookup floods are real risks.

today: RFC 4095 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3865, and the text itself says its usefulness depends on that extension becoming widely used.

sections.title: Why Keywords Need Meaning
sections.content:
RFC 3865 defines the solicitation class keyword: a label attached to an email message and carried by ESMTP. Keywords look like domain names written in reverse, for example com.example.adv. A sender can put them in a No-Solicit: header, and mail transfer agents can add them to trace fields.

RFC 3865 treats keywords as opaque and leaves their meaning out of scope. This RFC fills that gap. If keywords become widely used, one message might carry many of them, some from the sender, some required by regulators or recommended by industry associations, and some added along the delivery path. A reader needs a way to find out what each one means.

The stated design goal is to keep things as simple as possible. Defining an XML structure with metadata about the keyword, or any other format for the explanation, was ruled out. The system only associates a keyword with a URI, and the page at that URI carries the explanation.
sections.eli5: Imagine stickers on a package that say what is inside, but nobody told you what the stickers mean. This document says where to look up the meaning of each sticker.

sections.title: From Keyword to Lookup Name
sections.content:
The RFC uses the NAPTR resource record from the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS), and does one lookup from keyword to URI. It does not use the simplified S-NAPTR application, because S-NAPTR does not allow the U flag for terminal lookups or the regular expression field, and a replacement field can only hold a domain name while this application needs a URI.

To build the lookup key, the character . is substituted for any :, and then the keyword is reversed using . as the delimiter. So org.example:ADV becomes ADV.example.org.

Because domain names are case insensitive and : becomes ., the keywords com.example:ADV, com.Example:adv and com:example:ADV are syntactically equivalent for this application.

The result must also be a valid DNS name. Labels are limited to 63 characters and the total length must be less than 253 characters. Non-ASCII characters, including those after the :, must be encoded with the Internationalized Domain Names specifications in RFC 3490.
sections.eli5: The keyword is written backwards, like turning "Smith, Anna" into "Anna Smith", so it becomes an ordinary web-style name that can be looked up.

sections.title: How the NAPTR Fields Are Used
sections.content:
Each NAPTR field has a fixed role here. ORDER and PREFERENCE are processed as in RFC 3403: among records with a matching SERVICE, the ones with the lowest ORDER MUST be used, and of those the lowest PREFERENCE SHOULD be used. FLAGS MUST be U, SERVICES MUST be only no-solicit, and REPLACEMENT MUST be empty.

The REGEXP field MUST hold a valid URI. Per RFC 3402 it has a delimiter character, a regular expression, another delimiter, a replacement value and a final delimiter. Here the regular expression MUST be empty and the replacement value MUST be a valid URI as defined in RFC 3986. That URI SHOULD use the ftp, http or https scheme, and the document retrieved SHOULD conform to HTML 4.01, including its accessibility guidelines.

Wildcards are appropriate, so several keywords sharing a common prefix can point to one URI. The RFC warns that NAPTR is a subtyping record, so wildcards can have unintended effects when several types of NAPTR records are used, and implementors and zone administrators should take care.
sections.eli5: Each part of the DNS entry has a job. One part says "this is a no-solicit entry" and another holds the web address, like a contact card with a single link on it.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The example adds NAPTR records to the example.com zone for the keyword com.example.2795, which become records at 2795.example.com. Some answers have services such as iam+invalid or sip+invalid, which do not match no-solicit and are skipped. Matching records have ORDER and PREFERENCE values of 1 2, 2 1 and 1 1, and all point to http://infinite.example.com/keywordinfo.html. By the ordering rule, the record with order 1 and preference 1 wins.

A short, non-normative Perl script does the same steps: it replaces : with ., reverses the labels, queries NAPTR, discards records whose service is not no-solicit, sorts by order and preference, and prints the URI from the first record. Its comments note that DNSSEC checks belong before the answers are trusted. The page it fetches is a joke tied to RFC 2795: it says the message conforms to the spirit of that RFC.
sections.eli5: The example is a treasure hunt. Write the keyword backwards, ask the address book, pick the best entry and follow its link to a page that explains the keyword.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists four concerns.

  • If the DNS lookup is compromised, the URI may give wrong guidance. An https: URI without DNSSEC can create an unwarranted illusion of authenticity, and even with both, the client must check that the two signature contexts belong to the same domain owner.
  • RFC 3865 does not say whom to trust. A sender or intermediate MTA could insert a keyword and use this mechanism to mislead the recipient, for example with a made-up keyword such as org.example.certified.message suggesting official status.
  • Domain names are not persistent identifiers, so a name may later be controlled by someone else and give different results over time.
  • A malicious sender could insert many keywords, or badly formed ones, causing excessive DNS lookups. That could hit the provider at a given URI, or DNS registries and root servers if the keywords have non-existent top or second level domains.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write any sticker on a package, and a fake address book could point you to a fake page. So do not believe a label just because it sounds official.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA keeps no central registry of values for the NAPTR SERVICE field, so no direct IANA action is required. IANA does keep an Application Service Tag Registry for the S-NAPTR application of RFC 3958. This RFC advises IANA that the no-solicit value is in use here and should not be used in that registry for other applications.
sections.eli5: The name tag "no-solicit" is now taken, so nobody else should use it for something different.

cells: Lowest ORDER with matching SERVICE MUST be used; lowest PREFERENCE SHOULD be used
MUST hold a valid URI; the regular expression part MUST be empty
